title: Lenovo Revenue Jumps 43% to Record on AI Infrastructure Boom
excerpt: The world's largest PC maker posted its highest quarterly revenue growth in five years, with AI-related revenue reaching \.3 billion as shares surged to an all-time high.
body:
• Lenovo reported a 43% jump in quarterly revenue to $26.94 billion, beating analyst expectations of $22.3 billion
  • AI-related revenue grew 60% year-on-year to $9.3 billion, accounting for 35% of total revenue
  • Shares hit an all-time high with year-to-date gains of 225%, surging 17% after the results
  • A non-cash warrant revaluation loss of $1.7 billion pushed the company to a net loss despite record revenue

Lenovo Group reported its highest quarterly revenue growth in five years on Thursday, posting a 43% jump to $26.94 billion in the three months ended June 30, as the world's largest PC maker rides an artificial intelligence hardware boom and benefits from a global memory chip shortage.

The results smashed analyst expectations of $22.3 billion, sending shares of the Hong Kong-listed company surging as much as 17% after the announcement. Lenovo's stock had already hit an all-time high earlier in the session, bringing year-to-date gains to 225%.

AI Revenue Drives the Surge

At the heart of Lenovo's outperformance is its rapidly growing AI business. AI-related revenue grew 60% year-on-year to $9.3 billion, accounting for 35% of total revenue in the fiscal first quarter — a sharp increase from prior periods that underscores how deeply AI demand is reshaping the hardware industry.

The company's AI server pipeline reached $54 billion, up 157% quarter-over-quarter, reflecting surging demand from hyperscalers, AI cloud providers, and enterprise clients. R&D expenses jumped 30% year-on-year as Lenovo invests to keep pace with the AI infrastructure buildout.

"AI-related revenue grew 60% year-on-year to $9.3 billion, accounting for 35% of total revenue."

— Lenovo Q1 FY2027 Earnings Report

PC Division Holds Strong

Lenovo's PC, tablet, and smartphone division, which still accounts for about 64% of total revenue, reported a 27% year-on-year increase. The company retained its global market lead with a 25.6% share, according to Counterpoint Research, even as the broader PC market contracted 2% year-on-year to 16.6 million units — the first decline since early 2025, driven by memory-related cost pressures.

U.S. competitors Dell, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and Super Micro Computer have been among Wall Street's best performers this year but have raised prices by 10% to 30% due to soaring NAND and DRAM memory chip costs. Lenovo has also raised PC prices to mitigate the impact.

A Net Loss With an Asterisk

Despite the revenue beat, Lenovo swung to a net loss attributable to shareholders of $609 million, compared with a profit of $505 million a year earlier. Analysts had expected a profit of $589 million.

The company attributed the loss primarily to a non-cash fair value loss of $1.7 billion arising from the revaluation of warrants issued in 2025. Stripping out one-off items, adjusted net income more than doubled to $1.075 billion, suggesting the underlying business is performing well above expectations.

Riding the AI Infrastructure Wave

Lenovo's results come as the global technology industry grapples with simultaneous tailwinds and headwinds: surging AI infrastructure spending on one side, and a tightening memory chip supply chain on the other. The company warned earlier this year of pressure on PC shipments from the worsening memory shortage, but AI demand has more than offset those constraints.

The company's $54 billion AI server pipeline — up from prior quarters — positions it alongside Dell and Super Micro as a key supplier to the data centers powering large language models and AI applications. With AI-related revenue now exceeding a third of total sales, Lenovo's transformation from a PC-centric company to an AI infrastructure player is accelerating.
